mappings.note: Why biodiversity must be protected. The protect-the-environment outcome; not CG-SCI4 alone, because the item is about the reason for taking protective action.
Names the method of arranging things by common features as grouping. The classification outcome itself.
Ponds are the odd one out among terrestrial habitats. Sorting habitats into land and water classes, LO-3.
One hump in hot deserts, two in cold. A structural difference between two populations; LO-2 rather than LO-5, since the item asks what differs, not what the hump is for.
Which animal both flies and walks. Places a named animal in a movement-based group, LO-3.
Assertion-reason: streamlined body as adaptation because it aids swimming. The reason is the feature-to-habitat link, LO-5.

Which characteristics go with dicots. The answer turns on taproot plus two cotyledons against parallel venation, the monocot/dicot differentiation, LO-2. The stem carries only one of the three numbered statements its options reference.
A community-protected forest patch is a sacred grove. Community protection of the environment, LO-11.
The nature walk's objective is to experience the variety and beauty of nature. Sensitivity towards the living world, CG-SCI4; no LO covers appreciation as an aim.
Mimicked bird calls demonstrate that each bird has a unique chirp. Distinguishing organisms by an observable feature -- here sound -- is LO-1's register of appearance, texture, function and aroma.
Plants shorter than trees with woody stems near the ground are shrubs. The LO-3 category set.
Key difference between herb and shrub stems. The verb is 'differ' on the basis of stem structure, so LO-2 rather than the classification LO.
Hibernation is not a type of movement. Tests the boundary of the movement classification, LO-3.
Taproot plus net-like venation identifies a dicot. Applies the dicot/monocot differentiation to an unseen plant, LO-2.
Assertion-reason: long hair on Ladakh camels insulates against cold. The reason is the adaptation-to-habitat link, LO-5.
Which statements about bases for grouping plants are correct. The subject is what counts as a valid grouping basis, LO-3. Stem retains only one of the three numbered statements.
Wheat's single cotyledon predicts parallel venation and fibrous roots. The full monocot side of the differentiation, LO-2. Not LO-10: the farmer is scene-setting, nothing is applied to farming.
The year of the Cheetah Reintroduction Project. A conservation programme, LO-11.
Why not to pluck leaves and flowers -- leaving them for their ecological role and for others. A protective habit the student is asked to adopt, which is LO-11's own register.
Names the main-root-with-side-roots system as a taproot. Recognition from an observable structure, LO-1; no contrast with fibrous roots is required.
Banana leaves show parallel venation. Identifies a named plant's observable feature, LO-1.
The primary difference between terrestrial and aquatic habitats. The verb is 'difference', so LO-2, where item 63's sorting task was LO-3.
Which species have NOT declined through habitat loss. The subject matter is species decline through environmental damage, LO-11.
Net-like venation plus a splittable seed gives a dicot with taproots. The dicot/monocot differentiation applied to an unseen plant, LO-2.
Assertion-reason: sacred groves conserve biodiversity because communities prevent harm. Community environmental protection, LO-11.
Which features characterise trees -- height, woody stem, high branching. Defining an LO-3 category. The stem preserves only one of the three numbered statements.
One cotyledon plus parallel venation predicts fibrous roots in a newly discovered plant. The monocot differentiation, LO-2.
Save Silent Valley opposed a dam on the Kunthipuzha. An environmental protection movement, LO-11.
Wide hooves spread the camel's weight on sand. A feature explained by the demand of its habitat, LO-5.
The term for where organisms live together sharing resources. Habitat as the organising frame, LO-3, consistent with the other definition items in this chapter.
What 'dicot' stands for -- two cotyledons. Terminology tied to an observable seed feature, LO-1; no contrast is demanded, so not LO-2.
How a shrub stem differs from a tree stem on thickness and branching height. A structural differentiation, LO-2.
Photosynthesis is not an animal movement. Tests the boundary of the movement classification, LO-3.
Parallel venation and one cotyledon predict fibrous roots. The monocot differentiation, LO-2.
Assertion-reason where the reason (identical conditions everywhere) is FALSE; the student must know diversity follows from varied conditions and adaptation. That reasoning is LO-5.
Which features characterise herbs -- small, soft green stems. Defining an LO-3 category. Stem holds only one of the three numbered statements.

A tall woody plant with high branches and net-like veins is a tree with a taproot. LO-3 for placing it in the tree class and LO-2 for the reticulate-to-taproot inference; the item genuinely needs both.
The purpose of the Cheetah Reintroduction Project is to restore a lost population. Environmental protection, LO-11.
Who was invited for the nature walk. Pure narrative recall from the chapter's frame story; no LO applies, so cited at the goal the nature walk serves.
Maniram chacha mimics bird calls. Tied to the chapter's point that each bird has a distinctive call -- an observable feature used to tell organisms apart, LO-1.
The nature walk's stated objective, to experience nature's variety. Sensitivity to the living world, goal level; no LO covers it.
Each bird has a unique chirp. Distinguishing organisms by an observable feature, LO-1.
The term biodiversity. No outcome in this 13-item frame names biodiversity, so the goal carrying concern for life.
Whether plants and animals depend on each other. Interdependence as a process to be explained, LO-6; not LO-5, since no cause is sought.
Small plants with soft green stems are herbs. The LO-3 category set.
The pattern of veins is called venation. Naming an observable leaf feature, LO-1.
Net-like pattern about a thick midrib is reticulate venation. Identification from an observable feature, LO-1.
A bunch of similar thin roots from the stem base is fibrous. Identification from an observable structure, LO-1.
Reticulate venation generally goes with taproots. Holds the venation/root correlation, which is the LO-2 differentiation.
Dicots have two cotyledons. The cotyledon count is the monocot/dicot discriminator, LO-2.
Monocots generally have fibrous roots. The other half of the same differentiation, LO-2.
Names the features that let organisms survive in a region as adaptations. LO-5's own example is adaptations related to habitat.
The place where plants and animals live is a habitat. Habitat as the organising frame, LO-3, consistent with the other habitat definitions here.
Give one terrestrial habitat. Places an example in a habitat class, LO-3.
Animals living in water and on land are amphibians. Naming a habitat-based class, LO-3.
The 1973 project protecting the Bengal Tiger. A conservation programme, LO-11.
Community-guarded forest patches are sacred groves. Community environmental protection, LO-11.
Dr Raghu's advice to respect living creatures and observe without disturbing them. Sensitivity to life, CG-SCI4; LO-13's values are about honesty and cooperation among people, not toward organisms.
Three ways plants vary -- height, stem hardness, leaf shape and arrangement, flower colour and scent. That list is LO-1's observable-features register almost word for word.
How animals depend on plants and plants on animals, with an example each. Explaining a two-way ecological process, LO-6; not LO-5, since the item asks for the mechanism, not a cause.
